chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Khalid al-Qammam who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'For the foolish man who has lost his mind, is the divorce of his guardian valid over him?' He said: 'And why would he not be divorced by him?' I said: 'We cannot be sure that if he divorces her, he will not say tomorrow,

key_terms.الذَّاهِبُ الْعَقْلِ: One who has lost his mind/sanity
key_terms.الْأَحْمَقُ: The foolish man (a specific legal category of person with limited mental capacity, distinct from the completely insane)

ai.seo_question: Does the guardian of a foolish man have the authority to divorce him in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes that the guardian of a foolish man (al-ahmaq)—distinguished from the insane (majnun) by retained basic intellect but lacking financial prudence—holds authority equivalent to the ruler (sultan) to effect divorce. This ruling ensures legal stability by preventing the foolish man from invalidating the divorce through later claims of lack of intent or procedural ignorance, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that the guardian acts as a proxy for the state's authority in personal status matters.
